failures.title: BMW B58B30O0 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Cooling System Leaks - Plastic Vent Lines & Coolant Junctions
items.whatHappens: The Gen 1 B58 (B30M0/O0) uses plastic vent lines and coolant junctions that crack under heat cycles. The small plastic vent hose linking the oil filter housing to the expansion tank sits inches from sustained turbo heat, regularly swinging from ambient to over 220°F. When these crack, coolant loss is gradual and often goes unnoticed until overheating occurs. Left unaddressed, it can lead to warped cylinder heads or complete engine failure.
items.repairVsReplace: Replacement of the vent lines and coolant junctions is a manageable repair (£300-£800 at an independent specialist). However, if the engine has overheated due to prolonged coolant loss, the closed-deck block's reduced water jacket around the upper cylinders means heat damage can be severe - in those cases, a full reconditioned unit is often the safer bet. → Read our full cooling system failure guide

items.title: Oil Filter Housing Failure - Warping & Internal Collapse
items.whatHappens: The oil filter housing on Gen 1 B58 engines is plastic and can warp or fail internally under heat stress. This can cause oil filter disintegration, leading to oil starvation - a catastrophic failure on an engine with forged rods and a steel crank that transmits stress loads aggressively when oil pressure drops.
items.repairVsReplace: OFH replacement is a specialist job (£500-£1,000) but is far cheaper than a full engine. If the engine has been run with low oil pressure or a collapsed filter, bottom-end damage is likely - in which case replacement is the only option. → Read our full oil system failure guide

items.title: PCV Valve Failure - Integrated Design Problems
items.whatHappens: The B58's PCV valve is integrated into the valve cover. When the diaphragm tears (common on Gen 1 engines), crankcase pressure builds, causing oil leaks from seals and gaskets. Symptoms include a whistling noise from the engine, oil consumption, and visible leaks around the valve cover.
items.repairVsReplace: The PCV valve is integrated into the valve cover, so replacement requires a new valve cover assembly (£400-£800). If caught early, this is a straightforward repair. If ignored, oil leaks can lead to low oil levels and eventual bearing failure - at which point a replacement engine becomes the only viable solution.

failures.goodYearsLine: The B58B30O0 was replaced by the B58B30O1 (B58TU) from 2018 onwards, which introduced 350-bar direct injection, split cooling circuits, and a revised crank - but the plastic cooling and oil system components remained largely unchanged. Post-2018 TU1 engines have better fuel systems but share the same core cooling and PCV vulnerabilities.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the B58B30O0
variants.intro: The B58B30O0 is the original high-output Gen 1 B58 variant, distinguished from the earlier B58B30M0 by its higher 335 hp output (versus 322-326 hp in the M0). Unlike the later B58B30O1 (B58TU), the O0 uses a 200-bar direct injection system and lacks the split-cooling circuits introduced with the TU update. Where the code appears: - Stamped on a metal plate on the engine block (left-hand side, near the timing cover) - On the V5C logbook under "Engine number" (the first 8 characters will read B58B30O0) - Via BMW VIN decoder - the 7th character of the VIN indicates engine type Commonly confused with: - B58B30M0 - lower output (322-326 hp), fitted to earlier 340i/440i models (2015-2016) - B58B30O1 - B58TU successor with 350-bar fuel system, split cooling, 340-382 hp - S58B30O0 - full M-division engine, 473 hp, completely different engine

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement B58B30O0 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used B58B30O0 can make sense for lower-value F-series hosts where the car's value doesn't justify a recon unit. However, the Gen 1 B58's plastic cooling components and OFH are age-sensitive, so only consider a used unit with documented service history and evidence that the cooling system has been addressed. The biggest risk is buying an engine that's already suffered from slow coolant loss or PCV failure. Link once: /services/used-engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper B58B30O0 recon addresses the engine's known weak points: replacement of all plastic cooling lines and coolant junctions, OFH inspection or replacement, PCV valve/cover replacement, and new gaskets throughout. This is the sweet spot for most M240i, M140i, 340i and 440i owners - you get a fresh engine with the factory weaknesses engineered out, at a fraction of new OEM cost. Link once: /services/reconditioned-engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified when the original engine has suffered catastrophic failure (overheating, oil starvation) and the car is a keeper or low-mileage example. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, and a fully refreshed cylinder head - but this is specialist territory and typically only makes sense for high-value or performance-oriented hosts. Link once: /services/rebuilt-engines

buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The B58B30O0 typically sits in BMWs worth £8,000-£25,000 (F-series M140i, M240i, 340i, 440i). With a reconditioned supply cost of £3,800-£6,000, replacement is financially viable on most examples. For cars under £5,000, consider scrapping or breaking the vehicle before committing to a replacement.

mainEntity.name: What are the most common failures on the B58B30O0?

mainEntity.name: Should I buy a used or reconditioned B58B30O0 engine?

acceptedAnswer.text: A used unit can make sense for lower-value F-series cars (under £7,000) provided it has documented history and evidence of cooling system maintenance. However, a reconditioned engine is the safer long-term choice - it replaces all known weak points (cooling lines, OFH, PCV) and comes with a 12-24 month warranty. Used is cheaper but riskier; reconditioned addresses factory weaknesses and is the best value for most owners.

mainEntity.name: How do I confirm my car has the B58B30O0 and not another B58 variant?

acceptedAnswer.text: Check the engine code stamped on the block (left-hand side near the timing cover) - it will read B58B30O0. The V5C logbook also lists the full engine number, with the first 8 characters identifying the code. Common confusions: B58B30M0 (322-326 hp) and B58B30O1 (TU, 340-382 hp). Fitting the wrong revision is not a straight swap - ECU, fuel system and cooling differ.

mainEntity.name: How long does a B58B30O0 engine typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With correct servicing and early attention to cooling system maintenance, these engines regularly exceed 150,000 miles. The closed-deck block and forged internals are robust; the limiting factors are the plastic cooling components and PCV system. Preventative replacement of cooling vent lines at 60k miles is recommended. Strict adherence to BMW's Longlife-14 FE+ oil spec is critical.
